strengths: Novel and well-motivated formalization of 'multi-level non-IID' as a unifying framework subsuming slight/global, cluster-wise, and client-wise non-IID as special cases, filling a genuine conceptual gap in the FL literature.

The additive multi-level modeling idea (summing outputs from a hierarchy of global, cluster, and personalized models) is intuitive, and the level-wise alternating optimization with progressive level-adding and validation-based pruning is a practical and reasonably well-engineered training scheme.
Convergence analysis is provided for both the clustering (EM) sub-objective and the overall FL objective, giving some theoretical grounding for the alternating optimization procedure.

Extensive empirical evaluation across a good variety of synthetic non-IID regimes (cluster-wise with several cluster counts, Dirichlet client-wise, multi-level with different level/cluster configurations, and IID) on two datasets, with consistent gains over strong personalized/clustered FL baselines, ablations on level pruning, and visualizations comparing discovered vs. ground-truth relational structure.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility details in the appendix (hyperparameters, data partition construction, full algorithm listing, per-setting numerical tables), and an honest discussion of added storage/computation costs ('No Free Lunch' section).
weaknesses: The closest related prior work, clustered additive modeling (CAM, ref [34]), is discussed but never included as an empirical baseline in the main comparison table, which is a significant omission given the paper's central additive-modeling contribution and its claim of superiority over prior additive approaches with a 'fixed two-level' structure.

Evaluation relies entirely on synthetic partitions (cluster-wise and hand-constructed 'multi-level' splits) explicitly designed to match FeMAM's assumed hierarchical structure; there is no evaluation on a real-world dataset with organically hierarchical/non-synthetic client relationships (e.g., federated benchmarks with natural user hierarchies), which limits confidence that gains generalize beyond favorable synthetic settings.

The maximum number of levels L is fixed to 5 across all experiments as a hyperparameter and does not always match the true number of levels in the synthetic multi-level settings (e.g., 3 ground-truth levels); no sensitivity analysis of performance vs. L (beyond one qualitative table) or discussion of how a practitioner would choose L for real deployments where ground truth is unknown.

The convergence theorems require convexity and Lipschitz smoothness assumptions that are unrealistic for the ResNet-9 models actually used in experiments, so the theoretical guarantees provide limited practical assurance beyond motivating the alternating-minimization structure.

Only two (visually similar) image classification datasets and a single small client count (m=50) are studied, and results are averaged over only 4 runs; broader domains (e.g., text, tabular) or larger federations are not explored, limiting evidence of general applicability.

Presentation is dense in places (heavy, sometimes inconsistent notation across Sections 3-4 and the appendix, small/hard-to-read figures such as Fig. 4 and the structure-visualization figures), which could hinder reproducibility and comprehension for readers less familiar with the specific formalism.

strengths: Formalizes a novel and useful abstraction ('multi-level non-IID') that unifies global (FedAvg), cluster-wise, and client-wise personalized FL as special cases of a single additive hierarchy, which is conceptually clean and well motivated (Fig. 1).

The Multi-Level Additive Modeling (MAM) formulation, where a client's prediction is the sum of outputs from models assigned at each level, is an intuitive and interpretable extension of prior two-level additive/residual FL work (e.g., [18, 34, 35) to arbitrary depth.

Practical algorithmic design choices (progressive level-adding, freezing earlier levels, validation-based model pruning via Eq. 9) are sensible engineering solutions that address training instability and communication/computation cost, and are empirically shown to keep runtime and communication volume competitive with FedAvg/Ditto (Fig. 5).

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across four qualitatively different non-IID regimes (cluster-wise, client-wise/Dirichlet, multi-level, IID) on two datasets, with consistent gains over strong clustered- and personalized-FL baselines (FeSEM, PFedMe, FedRep, Ditto, etc.), plus ablations on level count and communication efficiency.

Nice qualitative analysis (Fig. 4, Appendix Fig. A.1/C.1/C.2) demonstrating that the learned multi-level structure (cluster assignment per level, pruned levels) recovers the pre-defined ground-truth relational structure, providing some interpretability beyond aggregate accuracy numbers.
A convergence analysis is attempted and proofs are provided in the appendix, giving at least a first-order theoretical grounding for the alternating level-wise optimization scheme.
weaknesses: The 'multi-level non-IID' benchmarks are synthetically constructed by the authors themselves to match the hierarchical structure the method is designed to exploit (Table C.1); there is no evaluation on a dataset with a real/naturally occurring multi-level structure, so the strongest reported gains (Table 1/C.4) may partly reflect a favorable match between benchmark design and method design rather than general superiority.

The convergence theorems (Theorems 1-2, Appendix D) rely on strong assumptions (convexity of the local loss, Lipschitz smoothness, bounded gradient variance, a 'compactness of mapping function' assumption) that are unlikely to hold for the ResNet-9 backbone actually used in experiments, so the theoretical guarantees provide limited practical assurance and the gap between theory and the non-convex experiments is not discussed.

Evaluation is restricted to two image-classification datasets (Tiny ImageNet, CIFAR-100) and a single backbone (ResNet-9); no experiments on other modalities (text/tabular) or larger/more realistic FL benchmarks (e.g., FEMNIST, Shakespeare) are provided, limiting evidence of general applicability.

Key structural hyperparameters (maximum level L=5, number of clusters K=5 per intermediate level, pruning threshold epsilon=0) are fixed a priori and not learned/searched, which is in tension with the claim that FeMAM 'automatically optimizes the knowledge-sharing structure'; only within-level pruning is adaptive, while the number of levels and per-level cluster counts are manually chosen and not validated via sensitivity analysis.

No systematic ablation or sensitivity study on the pruning threshold epsilon, the number of clusters K_l per level, or robustness to mis-specified L, despite these being central design knobs of the method.

Additional communication/storage/inference overhead from storing up to L-1 models per client is acknowledged only qualitatively in Appendix A ('acceptable for most smart devices') without a quantitative comparison of memory/inference cost against baselines, which is relevant for the claimed FL/edge-deployment setting.

Presentation has minor but noticeable issues (e.g., inconsistent citation label 'JFCA' vs 'IFCA', typo 'Chien-wise' in Fig. 1 caption, dense/cluttered small-multiple figures) that slightly hinder readability, though these do not affect the core claims.

strengths: Conceptually clean generalization of federated personalization from the common two-level (global+local) or fixed-cluster paradigm to an arbitrary-depth additive hierarchy, addressing a genuine gap in the literature where most clustered/personalized FL methods commit to a fixed granularity.

The grow-and-prune training protocol (boosting-style sequential level addition with client-specific pruning based on validation improvement) is a practical and well-motivated mechanism for avoiding the need to pre-specify hierarchy depth, and keeps per-round communication comparable to single-model FL.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three distinct non-IID regimes (cluster-wise, Dirichlet client-wise, and an explicitly constructed multi-level partition) on two image datasets, with consistent and often substantial improvements over strong clustered, personalized, and multi-model FL baselines.

A large-scale, contemporary experiment using LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-4B across 71 heterogeneous FLAN tasks demonstrates applicability beyond toy CNN settings and to foundation-model-style federated learning.

Thorough supplementary analyses: convergence/plateau visualization tied to level additions, learned-structure vs ground-truth comparisons, ablations on L and K showing robustness to hyperparameter choice, and cost/communication/storage analysis.
A convergence analysis is provided that combines per-level averaged-gradient guarantees with a boosting-style monotone descent argument across levels.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis relies on strong, somewhat post-hoc assumptions (e.g., Assumption D.4's bounded assignment slack εl and Assumption D.5's residual-alignment constant γl are simply posited to exist rather than derived from concrete conditions on the data/algorithm), making the 'convergence' guarantee closer to an interpretive narrative than a rigorous bound; the paper itself labels this 'convergence intuition.'

The main experimental instantiation only tests one specific composition of level-wise methods (FedAvg → K-means clustering → local training); despite the framework being pitched as generally composable with methods like IFCA, FedEM, Ditto, or FedPer at different levels, no such combinations are empirically explored, weakening the generality claims made in the introduction and related work.

The 'Multi-level non-IID' partition used to showcase FeMAM's core advantage is constructed explicitly to contain nested cluster structure at 3 distinct granularities, closely matching FeMAM's own architecture; this risks favorable bias toward the proposed method relative to a partition that was not designed with any particular algorithm's structure in mind.

Several directly relevant multi-level/hierarchical FL methods discussed in Related Work (Kim et al. 2022, Guo et al. 2024, Zhang et al. 2024, Briggs et al. 2020 hierarchical clustering) are not included as empirical baselines, so the claimed advantage over these specific multi-level competitors is argued conceptually but not verified experimentally.

Choosing which FL strategy to instantiate at each level, and the number/type of intermediate levels, itself constitutes a nontrivial design/hyperparameter search that is not automated, which partially undercuts the stated motivation of reducing the need for prior knowledge of task/heterogeneity structure.

Reported total training cost only accounts for per-round communication at the currently active level; the cumulative communication/computation across all sequentially trained levels (versus a single-model baseline) is not clearly quantified, and inference-time storage scaling with L, while discussed, is not benchmarked against actual latency in the large-scale foundation-model setting.

Statistical rigor is limited to mean ± std over 4 runs without significance testing, and the large-scale foundation-model results (Table 5) report only single point values without variance, despite earlier claiming multi-run averaging elsewhere.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine gap in existing clustered/personalized FL literature — most methods assume a fixed, pre-specified number of sharing granularities (global+cluster or global+client) — and proposes a principled generalization via a multi-level additive/residual hierarchy that removes the need to specify hierarchy depth a priori.

The grow-and-prune training protocol (boosting-style sequential level training with client-specific validation-based pruning) is a clean and practical mechanism that keeps communication and training cost comparable to single-model FL while allowing adaptive personalization depth per client.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three carefully designed non-IID regimes (cluster-wise, client-wise Dirichlet, and an explicitly constructed multi-level hierarchy) on two image benchmarks, with a good spread of strong and recent baselines (FeSEM, FedCAM, FedEM, pFedMoE, PM-MoE, Ditto), consistently shows FeMAM outperforming baselines, and importantly the method is not just strong on its 'home-turf' multi-level setting but also competitive on single-level settings where baselines specialize.

The paper provides interpretability analyses (Fig. 5, Fig. 8, Appendix Fig. A.1) showing the learned per-client model-count distributions and structure recovery against ground-truth cluster boundaries, which substantiates the claim that the method adaptively discovers heterogeneity structure rather than just fitting more parameters.
Cost analysis (wall-clock time, communication volume, inference model count) is thorough and demonstrates the method remains practical relative to baselines like Ditto/FedEM.

The large-scale foundation-model experiment (Qwen3-4B + LoRA across 71 real FLAN-T5 tasks) is a valuable addition showing relevance to contemporary FL-with-foundation-model settings beyond toy image classification.

A convergence analysis is provided that formalizes both within-level SGD convergence and monotone descent across levels via a boosting argument, giving some theoretical grounding to the empirical staircase convergence behavior observed in Fig. 4.
weaknesses: The convergence analysis relies on several strong and somewhat opaque assumptions (e.g., Assumption D.4's abstract bounded assignment slack ε_l, and D.5's boosting alignment constant γ_l ∈ (0,1]) that are not empirically estimated or validated, and whose relationship to the specific K-means/local-training instantiation used in experiments is only loosely justified; the theoretical results should be read mainly as convergence 'intuition' rather than a tight guarantee, which the authors themselves acknowledge but which somewhat overstates the paper's stated contribution of 'a convergence analysis.'

Despite the framework being advertised as flexible and able to incorporate different level-wise FL strategies (IFCA, FedEM, Ditto, FedPer, etc.), only a single instantiation (FedAvg → K-means clustering → local fine-tuning) is evaluated in the main experiments; the promised flexibility and its practical benefit (e.g., which combinations work best, or whether the choice matters) is not empirically explored, which is an acknowledged but still material limitation given it's a central selling point.

At inference time storage/compute can scale up to L-fold per client; although pruning mitigates this in practice, the worst-case cost and its scaling with larger L or bigger base models (especially relevant given the LLM experiments) is not stressed-tested.

The 'Multi-level non-IID' partition used for evaluation is constructed by the authors specifically to match the assumed hierarchical structure, which risks favoring the proposed method by design; while cluster-wise and client-wise (Dirichlet) partitions are more standard/neutral, the multi-level partition's realism and generality are less clearly established.

No code repository link or artifact is actually provided (the 'Code:' field in the abstract appears to be a placeholder), which is a reproducibility concern for a work with fairly complex training pipeline (server-side aggregation, per-level assignment rules, client-side pruning logic, multiple hyperparameters K, L per level).

The paper does not report standard deviations/error bars in some of the analysis figures (e.g., model-count distributions, structure visualizations) nor statistical significance testing between FeMAM and the closest baselines (e.g., PM-MoE on CIFAR-100 cluster-wise, where margins are small, ~52.6 vs 53.7).

Hyperparameter selection for K (fixed at 5) and L (fixed at 5) is justified mainly via limited ablation on one dataset/setting (Tiny ImageNet, client-wise) and may not generalize; sensitivity across a broader range of tasks/domains is not systematically studied.
